Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims
When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

vignette:
Priya is a 37-year-old South Asian woman who owns and operates a small clothing boutique in a mid-sized American city. She is married, describes her husband as supportive, and presents to therapy with a PCL-5 score of 72 - a level of severity that reflects how comprehensively her life has reorganised itself around a single event. Approximately fourteen months ago, Priya was sexually assaulted by a man she had been briefly involved with before her marriage, a former partner who had contacted her under the pretense of a business discussion and then forced himself on her in the back of a rideshare vehicle late one evening. The assault occurred in a confined, moving space from which she could not exit, with his body blocking hers against the seat. She remembers the pressure of being pinned, the particular angle of his face above her, the way the city lights slid past the window - and then a kind of dissolution, as though the experience exceeded what language could hold. To this day, Priya finds she cannot fully narrate what happened. The event sits in her not as a story she can tell but as something closer to sensation and image: a weight, a shadow, a smear of streetlight. She has tried to write it down and stopped each time, the words refusing to cohere into sequence.

In the weeks following the assault, Priya stopped taking public transport entirely. What had begun as an understandable aversion calcified into a fixed rule: she drives to the shop, drives home, and structures every errand around the availability of her own car. This avoidance has cost her concretely - a wholesale market she used to visit by train is now effectively inaccessible, and she has lost two supplier relationships as a result. She also began to notice herself becoming excessively agreeable in situations that felt even mildly pressured: with difficult customers, with delivery men who lingered too long, with any man whose tone sharpened. She recognised this as something she was doing to manage fear rather than because she meant it, but she could not stop. These strategies, rather than quieting the distress, kept her mind continuously circling the assault - the deliberate avoidance of transit and the performance of compliance both functioning as constant, low-grade reminders that something had happened that she was still trying to survive.

Priya's shop has become one of the most difficult arenas. She works behind a counter with her back to an open floor, and she had come to believe, with a certainty that felt bodily rather than rational, that she was unsafe unless she could see the entire room and feel a wall behind her. She rearranged the counter accordingly. When customers make sudden movements - reaching past her, turning quickly, dropping something - she is immediately on guard, her body bracing before her mind has registered what happened. These moments of perceived threat collapse the distance between the present and the assault: the vigilance pulls the memory forward, and the memory floods back with the same terror she felt in that car, not as recollection but as reliving. She suddenly feels as though it is happening again, and the guilt arrives with it - a corrosive sense that she should have refused the meeting, should have known, should have done something differently. She spends long stretches of the workday in a loop of counterfactual thinking, imagining the life that would have existed had she simply not replied to that message fourteen months ago.

The loop tightens in particular ways. The elevated threat she carries into each day means that ordinary sensory details - a customer who resembles one of the women she saw that night, hearing a name that sounds like his, a stranger mentioning an ex-partner in passing - land with disproportionate force, pulling her back into the memory and the terror it carries. The terror then amplifies her vigilance, which makes the next trigger harder to absorb. Her compliant, conflict-avoiding behaviour keeps her in situations she cannot fully control, and the avoidance of transport keeps her isolated in ways that prevent any disconfirmation of how dangerous the world now feels.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment in the shop three weeks ago when a male customer reached across the counter unexpectedly and she froze completely, unable to speak, shaking visibly until he left. Her husband had been watching. She is most afraid, she says, that she will never be able to tell the story of what happened to her - and most hoping that someone can help her find the words.
